content: Radial head fractures are the most common type of elbow fracture and typically occur as a result of falling onto an outstretched arm. In 1954, Mason classified these fractures into three types: type 1 (undisplaced fractures), type 2 (simple displaced fractures), and type 3 (comminuted fractures). Aspiration of the elbow joint is a procedure that aims to reduce intra-articular pressure and has been used as an initial treatment option for radial head fractures. However, this technique is invasive and carries risks, including potential infection and injury to surrounding nerves and blood vessels. The objective of this study was to evaluate the benefits and harms of elbow joint aspiration as a treatment for radial head fractures in adults. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, as well as trial registries, bibliographies, and conference proceedings. The search was completed on April 14, 2014. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled clinical trials that compared aspiration with no aspiration in the treatment of radial head fractures in adults. Two independent reviewers selected studies, assessed the risk of bias, and extracted data. Disagreements were resolved through discussion. When appropriate, results from comparable studies were pooled using fixed-effect meta-analysis. Two trials involving a total of 126 participants were included in the review, although results were only available for 108 participants. Most participants were adults over the age of 30. Both trials were assessed as having a high risk of bias in terms of selection, performance, detection, and reporting. Due to these limitations, the quality of evidence was downgraded by two levels, with an additional downgrade for imprecision. As a result, the evidence for all outcomes was judged to be of very low quality, meaning there is significant uncertainty regarding the findings. One trial included participants with Mason type 1, 2, or 3 radial head fractures, as well as a few cases of traumatic elbow hemarthrosis without fracture. The other trial included participants with Mason type 1 and 2 fractures. All participants were managed non-surgically. Neither trial reported functional outcomes using validated patient-reported measures of function or pain, such as a visual analogue scale. The evidence suggests that there is little difference between aspiration and no aspiration in terms of impaired function (e.g., inability to carry heavy loads or discomfort when carrying loads) at 12 months. Specifically, 9 out of 51 participants in the aspiration group reported impaired function compared to 7 out of 57 in the no-aspiration group (risk ratio 1.43 favoring no aspiration, 95% confidence interval 0.57 to 3.58). This finding is based on very low-quality evidence from two trials involving 108 participants. There is very low-quality evidence suggesting that aspiration may provide immediate pain relief following the procedure. Additionally, one trial involving 28 participants reported less pain at three weeks in the aspiration group, but it is unclear whether this benefit persists beyond that time point. Neither trial reported adverse events such as nerve or vascular injuries or infections. However, aspiration was unsuccessful in three participants (7.9%) in one trial. In terms of range of motion, very low-quality evidence indicates little difference between the aspiration and no-aspiration groups at six weeks (28 participants, one trial) or 12 months (108 participants, two trials). One trial involving 80 participants reported the absence of specific complications, including myositis ossificans, joint instability, and late displacement of the fracture. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness of joint aspiration as an initial treatment for radial head fractures in terms of function, pain, and range of motion. Additionally, the safety of the procedure remains unclear due to incomplete reporting of adverse events. Future research should include a detailed examination of current aspiration practices, prospective collection of adverse event data, and consultation with patients to understand their preferences and values. These steps would help guide the design of a multicenter randomized trial to provide definitive evidence on the use of aspiration for treating radial head fractures.
